sources.title: SRAC 479b Columnaris Disease: A Bacterial Infection Caused by Flavobacterium columnare

facts.fact: 'Mouth fungus' is not a fungal disease. It is a bacterial infection that needs antibacterial treatment.
The cause is Flavobacterium columnare, formerly called Flexibacter columnaris, so the disease is also called columnaris.
F. columnare is a Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacterium that moves by gliding and has no flagella.
In principle columnaris can affect all freshwater fish. It has been found in neon tetra, platy, zebrafish and koi.
In the acute form, skin lesions spread within hours, and up to 50% of a population may die within 36 hours.
In the chronic form, white lesions grow slowly and fish die only after a long course.
The disease is highly contagious, and young fish are especially vulnerable.
If left untreated, the bacteria can eat away the lip cartilage, so the fish starves or the infection spreads through the body.
Most cases develop slowly, but some strains act much faster and can kill within a few days.
Look for short off-white to grey tufts, mostly on the head, face, gills and jaws, sometimes on the body and fins.
True fungus looks different: long, white, fluffy threads like cotton wool. Columnaris tufts are short.
Columnaris is easily confused with fin rot, but its short tufts are distinctive.
In fish with scales, lesions may start at the fin margins and spread inward into a saddle shape, which is why it is called 'saddleback disease'.
In scaleless fish, the skin lesions are bluish-grey and dead, with a reddish margin.
Fin edges break down until the fin rays are exposed.
Gill filaments break down from the tips toward the gill arches, which cuts oxygen uptake and causes rapid breathing.
Saddleback lesions start at the base of the dorsal fin and spread from there.
Acute cases can kill fish before any signs show on the surface.
Mouth form: swollen lips with a white-grey, cotton-like film at the edges of the mouth. Later the jaw erodes and deep red ulcers stop the fish from closing its mouth.
Sick fish become lethargic, hide in corners or lie on the bottom, and stop eating.
In koi, gill rot caused by columnaris must be told apart from KHV, which also erodes the gills.
Under the microscope, fin tissue shows bacteria attached at one end and swaying, forming column- or haystack-like clusters. PCR is faster and more sensitive than culture.
The bacteria are normally present in aquaria and are opportunists. They invade wounds from fighting or fin-nipping.
Ammonia or nitrite above zero is strongly associated with outbreaks. Stress and a poor diet also weaken immunity.
Infection is favoured by poor water quality, high ammonia, high pH and low oxygen.
In culture the bacterium grows at 18–30 °C, and not below 14 °C or above 33 °C. Pond outbreaks peak in summer.
The bacterium is more virulent at 85–90 °F. At high temperatures, fish can die within hours.
Risk rises with a high bioload, overcrowding and low dissolved oxygen. The bacteria may survive in water for up to 32 days when hardness is 50 ppm or more.
Higher-risk fish include injured or nipped fish, cichlids that wrestle with their jaws, livebearers kept in soft acidic water, bettas kept unheated, and goldfish in unfiltered or overstocked tanks.
The bacteria thrive in water above 15°C, and infection spreads faster the warmer the water. Uneaten food and organic matter feed the outbreak.
Stress on the fish population drives outbreaks, and reducing stress lowers how often columnaris occurs.
Treat immediately, because the disease can move fast.
Move the sick fish to a separate tank or tub with strong aeration.
As a first step, give a medicated bath and lower the water temperature to about 24 °C (75 °F).
Use antibiotics effective against Gram-negative bacteria, such as kanamycin. The source gives no dose.
Phenoxyethanol at 100 mg/l for 7 days.
Nifurpirinol (furanace) at 0.2 mg/l for up to 5 days. It can harm the filter bacteria.
Salt is of little use as a treatment. Up to 1 oz per US gallon may help prevent infection, but only in salt-tolerant fish such as guppies and mollies.
Choose antibiotics based on a susceptibility test (antibiogram) and always fix husbandry at the same time.
Because the bacterium prefers alkaline water, lowering pH to 6.8 may support treatment.
Tetracyclines and quinolones are used. Medicated feed with oxytetracycline works for internal infection, but resistance is emerging.
Potassium permanganate, copper sulfate and hydrogen peroxide can be used externally, but they are toxic at high concentrations.
Hobby protocol from Vietnam: Furan-2 or ciprofloxacin plus salt at 3‰ (3 g per litre) for 4–5 days, with a 50% water change and fresh medicine every day.
Ulcers can be dabbed for a few seconds with a cotton swab soaked in povidone-iodine or diluted hydrogen peroxide. Then return the fish to the medicated water.
For early koi gill rot, one koi site gives a salt bath of 100 g per 4.5 litres (1 gallon) for 10 minutes. This is a very strong bath, so check it before use.
Pond treatment for koi: chloramine-T at 1 g per 4,500 litres (1,000 gallons). It is risky in soft water.
Pond treatment for koi: potassium permanganate at 1.5 g/1,000 litres, said to suit soft water better. The page's gallon figure does not match the litre figure.
For severe mouth infections in koi, take a swab for testing and pick the antibiotic from the result. It is often injected because the fish cannot eat.
Potassium permanganate is listed as an external treatment for columnaris.

1) Isolate the fish in a well-aerated tank. 2) Give the medicated salt bath with daily 50% water changes and re-dosing for 4–5 days. 3) Dab the ulcers. 4) When healed, change 30% of the water weekly and lower the salt gradually.
During recovery, feed fine powdered food, newly hatched Artemia or other soft food that is easy to swallow.
Cycle the tank before adding fish, keep it filtered, avoid overstocking and feed a balanced, vitamin-rich diet.
Keep compatible species, and keep fish that fight or nip apart.
Siphon out debris and change water on a steady schedule.
Leave no uneaten food, keep dissolved oxygen up and control ammonia and nitrite. Watch fish closely when the temperature rises.
A live attenuated vaccine exists for catfish.
Relying on salt as the main treatment is a mistake.
Letting uneaten food rot on the bottom and overcrowding the tank both help the disease spread.
Using chloramine-T in soft water can harm koi.
In Vietnamese the disease is commonly called 'nấm miệng'. The fish most often affected in Vietnamese home tanks are guppies (cá bảy màu), mollies and neon tetras.
Products used in Vietnam include Furan-2, ciprofloxacin, coarse salt (muối hột) and povidone-iodine.
During Hanoi heat waves, air can pass 38–40°C and pond water can reach 30–34°C. This is the most dangerous period of the year, with low oxygen.
In striped catfish (cá tra), the related disease called 'trắng đuôi' (white tail) occurs all year but is most common at the start of the rainy season.
Calling it a fungus is wrong. Chewy, Sài Gòn Cá Cảnh and others say it is a bacterial disease.
The name 'cotton wool disease' causes confusion with true fungus.
Tea-tree oil may help prevent infection in an injured fish that has been isolated.
One Vietnamese koi site says the cotton-wool 'mouth rot' it describes is probably caused by Aeromonas hydrophila, not columnaris.
